title: under the water and back up
hookLine: a baby in a white gown, a teenager in a pool: same word, an old disagreement

cards: A baby in a long white gown, a little water poured over her head while the grandparents take photos. A teenager in a T-shirt, held by the shoulders and leaned back into a pool, coming up to cheering.
Same word for both: baptism. Same faith. And a disagreement, centuries old, about when and how to do it.

teach.b: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, to plunge, to immerse. It's older than the church.
A wild preacher named John was dipping people in the Jordan River as a sign of turning their lives around, and Jesus himself walked into that river and was baptized.
Later he sent his friends out to baptize, and from the start, baptism was how someone joined. So why two pictures?

Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize babies. The idea: God's promise comes first, before the child can answer, and the family promises to raise them in it.
Baptist, Pentecostal and many non-denominational churches baptize people old enough to say yes for themselves, usually all the way under.
Paul's picture fits that well: down into the water like a burial, up like rising from the dead.

teach.h: A SIGN, OR THE MOMENT ITSELF.
teach.b: Whether baptism itself saves is a real difference too. Many churches call it the moment God makes a person new. Many others call it an outward sign of something God has already done inside.
Either way, the shape is the same.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize infants (by pouring, sprinkling or, in Orthodox churches, immersion); Baptist, Pentecostal and many non-denominational churches baptize believers, usually by full immersion. Almost all baptize once, in water, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

games.q: a family brings a newborn to a Methodist church to be baptized. what's the idea behind baptizing a baby?
o: the baby has chosen the faith.
God's promise comes first, before the child can answer.
games.why: in churches that baptize babies, the gift comes before the answer, and the family promises to raise the child in it.

games.q: put the picture back in order.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, breathe all the way out, slowly, like going under. On the second, pause a moment in the stillness before you breathe in.
On the third, breathe in deep, like coming up into the air. Notice how that first breath feels.

wordCard.voice: Baptism. From the Greek for dip or plunge: the way into the church, with water. Fourth word.

orig.note: Greek: to dip, to plunge, to immerse.

carryVoice: Your line: under the water, up again. A white gown or a T-shirt in a pool, it's the same picture. Day four.
